items.summary: Separable nonlinear least squares problems arise in inverse problems such as semi-blind image deblurring, where the image enters the forward model linearly, and the blur parameters enter nonlinearly. Even when the image is regularized, joint estimation of the image and blur parameters can favor a degenerate no-blur solution, in which the blur operator tends to the identity and the reconstruction merely denoises the data without removing the blur. We address this by regularizing the blur parameters. Motivated by the determinant term arising from Gaussian marginalization, we construct a family of blur-parameter priors whose weight and auxiliary operators can be chosen independently of the image prior. The resulting log-determinant penalty is incorporated into regularized variable projection, which eliminates the image variables by minimization. Under periodic boundary conditions and assuming the matrices involved admit a joint spectral decomposition, we show that a sufficiently large determinant weight rules out the no-blur solution as a local minimizer. We also characterize the regularizer's behavior as the auxiliary regularization scale tends to zero or infinity. We solve the reduced problem with a quasi-Newton method that evaluates the objective and its derivatives in the Fourier domain. In experiments with Gaussian, defocus, and motion blur, the proposed prior improves image and blur recovery over Gaussian marginalization across several settings, with determinant weights computed from the true image. A single-sample experiment illustrates how to automatically choose parameters from the data using a conditional generalized cross-validation criterion.
items.title: Marginalization-Based Regularization for Separable Nonlinear Least Squares Problems with Applications to Semi-Blind Deblurring

items.summary: Reconstruction of three-dimensional vascular structures from a limited number of X-ray projections is a severely underdetermined and ill-conditioned inverse problem. This work presents a unified matrix-free computational framework for evaluating iterative numerical methods for sparse-view cone-beam tomography. Forward and backprojection are implemented from ray-voxel intersection lengths computed with the Amanatides-Woo traversal algorithm, avoiding explicit construction of the large sparse system matrix. We systematically compare ART, SART, SIRT, gradient descent (GD), and Krylov subspace methods, including Conjugate Gradient, LSQR, and GMRES. The common matrix-free operators and geometry are used for all methods, allowing consistent comparisons under matched conditions. Particular emphasis is placed on gradient scaling using scalar step sizes, Jacobi preconditioning, and diagonal Hessian majorization, together with L1, Tikhonov, and total variation regularization. Numerical experiments use five three-dimensional coronary vessel models reconstructed from ten simulated X-ray projections under noise and scattering conditions, and are extended to real X-ray projections of a static thin-vessel phantom. Performance is evaluated in terms of convergence, computational cost, volumetric overlap, contrast-to-noise ratio, vessel diameter and centerline errors, and projection consistency at an unseen viewing angle. The results show that total-variation-regularized gradient descent with diagonal majorization provides the best overall reconstruction performance within the investigated computational budgets. By contrast, the tested Krylov implementations achieve limited geometric recovery despite higher computational cost. These findings emphasize the importance of appropriate gradient scaling and regularization for stable and computationally efficient sparse-view tomographic reconstruction.
items.title: Comparative analysis of numerical methods for X-ray 3D reconstruction from sparse views

items.summary: MELITE is an open-source Python package for the evaluation and selection of supervised classification and regression models using numeric tabular datasets. It supports classification-only, regression-only, and mixed-task workflows. Model evaluation uses task-specific cross-validation strategies and selection criteria: F1-macro for classification and RMSE for regression. Supported models are optimized with Optuna when hyperparameter tuning is applicable. Evaluation results, optimization summaries, and provenance are preserved in task-specific artifacts. Selected models can be fitted on the full dataset, exported, and reused for prediction. The resulting evaluation evidence supports reproducible model comparison but does not establish external predictive generalizability.
items.title: MELITE — Multi-Model Supervised Learning Evaluator

items.summary: Existing generative model-based approaches to linear inverse problems typically use the acquired noisy measurement to condition or guide sampling in the image domain. In this work, we introduce Dual Flow, a novel joint flow model for solving linear inverse problems by jointly estimating the clean image and its corresponding noise-free measurement from the observation. Specifically, Dual Flow formulates image reconstruction and measurement denoising as a coupled estimation problem, using coupled flows in the image and measurement domains. The acquired noisy measurement $\mathbf{y}_0$ is used only to initialize the measurement state; thereafter, the image and measurement states are jointly updated based on their current values. By construction, the final image and measurement estimates are guaranteed to satisfy the underlying forward model. We derive the sampling updates for the joint flow and show that they are governed by the conditional mean of the clean image given the current joint state. We further derive a closed-form expression for a sufficient statistic of the joint state and show that the required conditional mean can be obtained by solving an image-domain Gaussian denoising problem involving operator-dependent, correlated noise. We train a velocity-prediction network using this formulation to estimate the conditional mean from the derived sufficient statistic. Dual Flow requires no hyperparameter tuning beyond selecting the number of inference steps and achieves substantially shorter reconstruction times than competing methods. Extensive experiments across various linear inverse problems and image datasets demonstrate state-of-the-art performance in both distortion metrics and perceptual quality. Additional analyses assess robustness to model mismatch, as well as the ability to generate diverse plausible reconstructions and characterize reconstruction uncertainty.
items.title: Dual Flow: Joint Image-Measurement Flow for Inverse Problems

items.summary: Bragg Coherent Diffraction Imaging (BCDI) relies on phase retrieval (PR), a non-convex, ill-posed inverse problem whose conditioning is degraded by factors like noise, partial coherence, and strain or crystallographic defects in the imaged nanocrystal. Conventional approaches, including alternating projections and deep learning methods, represent the object on a dense voxel grid, which is prone to amplitude-phase mixing and becomes increasingly ill-posed under these factors, often preventing reliable three-dimensional mapping of the particle's shape and strain. Here we present ConvexAD, a gradient descent PR model that parametrizes the object shape as a convex polyhedron, built by the intersection of half-spaces and enforces flat amplitude within it by construction. This geometric regularization eliminates amplitude-phase mixing and reduces the number of trainable parameters, hence facilitating the convergence of the PR. Implemented in JAX for native GPU acceleration and forward-model flexibility, ConvexAD is validated on simulated and experimental BCDI data, where it outperforms conventional and deep learning assisted PR at high strain, low signal, and reduced coherence, extending the conditions under which quantitative BCDI reconstruction is achievable.
items.title: ConvexAD: differentiable phase retrieval with geometric regularization for high-strain, low-signal Bragg coherent diffraction imaging

items.summary: Nonlinear root-finding, analytic signal extrapolation, and Marchenko inverse scattering share a common mathematical bottleneck: the inversion of ill-posed linear or linearized operators that suffer from spectral clustering, numerical instability, and spurious pole proliferation in unconstrained continuous spaces. Projecting these systems onto the maximal class-number-one Heegner modular curve establishes a unique factorization domain that eliminates fractional holonomy phase slips, preventing branch-cut bifurcations and suppressing spurious pole-zero doublets. Truncating the singular modulus expansion at its principal term provides an analytical starting anchor that strictly satisfies Smale point-estimate convergence criteria, placing the system directly within the quadratic attraction basin and reaching machine precision in a single iteration. In analytic continuation, the modular coordinate under the maximal discriminant is suppressed well below double-precision machine epsilon, truncating out-of-band noise and bypassing the Runge phenomenon without empirical regularization parameters. For high-dimensional networks and discretized scattering kernels, operator preconditioning via Lubotzky–Phillips–Sarnak Ramanujan graph Laplacians enforces a uniform spectral gap derived from the Deligne bound on Hecke operators. This holds the condition number on the invariant zero-mean subspace to a small, constant bound, ensuring that both the Newton Jacobian update and the Marchenko integral equation converge in very few Krylov iterations regardless of network scale.
items.title: Arithmetic Operator Inversion: Resolving Nonlinear Root-Finding, Analytic Extrapolation, and Inverse Scattering via Heegner Modular Uniformization and Ramanujan Preconditioning

items.summary: Supplementary material and reproducibility package for the article Probing Coherent Noise with Stabilizer Codes: Identifiability, Ambiguity, and Decoder Priors . The supplement analyses the null result of a recent repetition-code experiment (arXiv:2606.07377), in which the logical fidelity of d = 3 and d = 5 bit-flip repetition codes was found to be indistinguishable under coherent and stochastic error injection, contrary to the circuit-level simulation of that work. It establishes three results, each independently checkable: The average gate infidelity of a coherent rotation is exactly invariant under randomization of its rotation axis by a drifting frame phase, so no fidelity-based comparison can detect such randomization at all. For a bit-flip repetition code read out in the computational basis, an X-type coherent injection and a stochastic injection of equal single-site average fidelity give logical error probabilities that agree to machine precision (3×10 −15 ), for d = 3 and d = 5, R = 10 rounds, with and without syndrome misreports. The gap reported in the experiment therefore cannot originate in coherent accumulation on the data qubits. The coherent–stochastic gap obeys [1 + (N−1)ρ]/N with ρ = <cos Δφ> = exp(−σ φ 2 ). The frame-phase spread required for the drift hypothesis to apply (σ φ ≳ 1.5 rad) lies a factor 30 outside the parameter domain of the generator model and an order of magnitude outside the small-angle domain in which the leading-order polarization expansion is formulated. The role of the companion's channel-level generator recovery is stated explicitly, in a dedicated section: it supplies the parameter (a static frame offset is δ i , with |δ i | ≤ 0.05 rad), the ε 2 /ε 4 order counting that makes the code orientation a choice of sensitivity, and the estimator itself; this note supplies the temporal question that the companion does not answer. The role of the companion's channel-level generator recovery is stated explicitly, in a dedicated section: it supplies the parameter (a static frame offset is delta_i, with |delta_i| <= 0.05 rad), the eps^2/eps^4 order counting that makes the code orientation a choice of sensitivity, and the estimator itself; this note supplies the temporal question that the companion does not answer. The supplement closes with a channel-level ratio, coh(R_code)/coh(R_ref), that would settle the question with data of the size already recorded. Contents. supplementary_material.pdf (9 pp., 5 figures, 2 tables) and its LaTeX source; five 400 dpi figures; Python code (numpy / scipy / matplotlib) that regenerates every figure and every quoted number from a single entry point; all generated data files in JSON; README with the model assumptions, the limitations, and the relation to the two source papers. Code is released under the MIT licence; text, figures and data under CC BY 4.0.

items.summary: Open-Source Moon: A Technical Framework for Intelligent Development of Extraterrestrial Bodies Based on Sensor Dispersal and Golden Consensus Abstract: The exploration and development of the Moon and other celestial bodies currently depend heavily on State-led, integrated space missions that are costly, slow, and difficult for the public to join. To address this situation, this paper proposes “Open-Source Moon”, a technical framework that applies the open-source philosophy to the intelligent development of extraterrestrial bodies. The framework treats the Moon as a large developer platform that all of humankind can program collectively. Following the progressive principle of “information first, from the outside in, from sensing to action”, it transforms the Moon layer by layer into a “smart planet” that can be programmed as a whole, and it organizes global participation through open-source protocols and the contribution-securing mechanism of “Golden Consensus”: massive numbers of low-cost, standardized micro sensors are first dispersed over the lunar surface to form a distributed sensing network whose nodes are beacons and hotspots; delay-tolerant networking (DTN) and a predictive compensation mechanism then overcome the one-way communication delay of about 1.28 s; and a small-machine cooperation ecosystem, LEGO-style combination of medium-sized machines, and finally unmanned factories and lunar computing carry the staged evolution from sensors to a “smart planet”. Based on the self-similar allocation principle and the Schelling focal point, which secure and incentivize decentralized contributions, a “Golden Consensus” system founded on the golden ratio ( φ ≈ 1.618) is proposed: explorers receive 61.8% of the development-rights return (of which a further 2.8% is set aside as a “common allocation” for public facilities), and 38.2% is designated as socially shared. A model with 880 000 cornerstone nodes is set up, in which a distributed ledger establishes ownership of contributions and keeps tamper-proof records. Verifiable engineering models of network coverage, link budget, energy budget, and delay compensation are established, and the compatibility of this approach with the 1967 Outer Space Treaty, as well as the general applicability of extending it to other celestial bodies such as Mercury and Mars, is demonstrated. This study provides a feasible technical route and governance framework for public participation in the development of extraterrestrial bodies. Keywords: Lunar Landing; Human Lunar Landing ; Open-Source Moon; sensor network; smart planet; Golden Consensus; delay-tolerant networking; lunar development; citizen science; Outer Space Treaty; Human Spaceflight 1. Introduction 1.1. Background and Motivation For more than half a century, the exploration of extraterrestrial bodies has taken the form mainly of large, integrated, State-led missions. After Apollo 17 in 1972, crewed spaceflight remained confined to near-Earth orbit for a long time, until Artemis II completed a crewed lunar flyby (without landing) in April 2026 [1]. On 22 February 2024, the Odysseus lander of Intuitive Machines achieved the first soft landing on the Moon by a commercial spacecraft [2], marking the beginning of the era of commercial lunar landings. However, the development and launch cost of a single mission is still on the order of tens of millions to hundreds of millions of US dollars, and most of the failure risk is concentrated in the powered-descent and landing phases. From the soft landing of Chang’e-3 in 2013 to June 2025, there were 14 soft-landing attempts on the lunar surface worldwide (Table 4): six full successes, three partial successes (in which the attitude or mission capability was impaired after landing), and five failures. According to public reports retrieved for this study, no new lunar landing attempt had occurred

items.summary: Repeated mobile GUI tests can reuse routes, locators, and recovery strategies from earlier executions. However, a route that worked in one workflow or app version may be irrelevant or misleading in another. We study how an LLM-based tester can retain useful experience while withholding entries contradicted by current observations. We present a maintenance contract for AdaptiTest in which reusable experience has an explicit applicability scope, trace provenance, and a lifecycle for confirmation, revalidation, and withdrawal. The contract reserves persistence for a Reflector role and treats recalled experience as advice. The archived implementation does not establish end-to-end enforcement of every specified mechanism. The design changes retrieved context, not model weights. The evaluation uses read-only Android workflows and archived internal comparisons. A six-task, three-repeat ready subset reports 18/18 completed runs with memory versus 3/18 without it, but a grounded single-agent control also solves the earlier hard-task slice. A separate cross-session probe is excluded from efficacy conclusions because of confounded route schedules and unvalidated state labels. We examine 13 selected real-update hazard records across nine subjects, distinguishing stale-locator observations from policy-based withholding and offline retrieval diagnostics. The latter do not measure live-device failures or actions saved. These events are UI changes, not confirmed regression bugs. The evidence supports a bounded design and case study; it does not establish general efficacy, superiority over independent GUI-agent systems, or unrestricted exploration.
items.title: Can LLM Agents Learn to Test? Maintaining Scoped Experience as Testing Evidence for Mobile GUI Testing

items.summary: MELITE is an open-source Python package for the evaluation and selection of supervised classification and regression models using numeric tabular datasets. It supports classification-only, regression-only, and mixed-task workflows. Model evaluation uses task-specific cross-validation strategies and selection criteria: F1-macro for classification and RMSE for regression. Supported models are optimized with Optuna when hyperparameter tuning is applicable. Evaluation results, optimization summaries, and provenance are preserved in task-specific artifacts. Selected models can be fitted on the full dataset, exported, and reused for prediction. The resulting evaluation evidence supports reproducible model comparison but does not establish external predictive generalizability.

items.summary: We describe our approach to the LUMPI track of the UrbanTwin Sim2Real LiDAR Challenge, in which a 3D object detector must be trained exclusively on synthetic data and evaluated on unseen real roadside LiDAR, while the synthetic point clouds are simultaneously scored for distributional realism. Our final entry scores 0.4793 combined, from a detection mAP of 0.1333 and a realism score of 0.9126. Our contribution is not a new architecture. Working from a PointPillars baseline, we obtained most of our gains from three sources. First, a diagnosis that small object failure in roadside LiDAR is a localisation problem rather than a detection problem, which led to a parameter free geometric refinement worth 86 percent relative on pedestrian AP. Second, an audit of our own post processing which revealed that a shipped rule was destroying valid predictions, the repair of which produced our single largest detection gain at 335 percent relative on the Van class. Third, treating the realism metrics analytically rather than as a black box, which showed that one of the four components is a closed form function of nine summary statistics. We also report an experimental methodology that we believe is the more transferable result. Because mean AP decomposes into independent per class terms, a single submission can carry several mutually controlled experiments, and a submission assembled entirely from previously measured components has a score that is known before it is sent. We predicted our final score to four decimal places prior to submission. We report negative results at equal length, and give a full account of data provenance and compliance in Section 8, including a full account of every mechanism contributing to the submitted score.

items.summary: Unrefereed research candidate. The isolated Kalman filter (IsoKF) of Jung, Luft and Weiss (Autonomous Robots, 2025) lets the nodes of a robot or sensor network share an estimation task cheaply: only the nodes involved in a measurement update, and their correlations with everyone else are rescaled by a correction factor. Its authors conjectured that for any completely observable and controllable system the covariance it reports converges to a finite, unique, stable steady state. Result: the conjecture is false. A three-node system with pair-sum observations x1+x2, x2+x3, x3+x1 and dynamics A = 3I is observable from one epoch and controllable, every local block the filter uses stays positive definite, yet the reported marginal variances satisfy m_k ≥ (5/4)(9/5)^k − 1/4, while the centralised Kalman filter keeps every variance at most 3/4. A Perron-root comparison extends divergence to every connected non-bipartite pair-sum graph when a^2 is large enough; extra attenuation or deletion of cross-covariances does not help. Schur-stable dynamics always give bounded marginals (proved). Computer-assisted proofs (outward-rounded interval arithmetic) show that for a^2 in (1, 1.38] large priors diverge at rate a^(2k), entry certified from 10^12 I at eight values down to a^2 = 1 + 10^-8, and that at a^2 = 21/20 the prior I converges while 10^12 I diverges: there is no globally attracting steady covariance. Also: exact classification of participant overlaps (|U ∩ V| ≤ 1) that keep every local block positive definite, and a bounded regime for anchored relative measurements. Scope: in high-precision numerical tests the actual estimation error stays bounded; the failure is gross pessimism of the reported covariance, not divergence of the estimate. The counterexample uses pair-sum measurements, not plain differences. Nothing is proved for a^2 in (1.38, 2+√5); uniqueness for stable dynamics remains open. The ikf_lib software was inspected but not run; no software failure is claimed. Version 0.2.0 (correction). Version 0.1.0 compared this work with Luft, Schubert, Roumeliotis and Burgard (2018, IJRR, doi:10.1177/0278364918760698) at abstract level only. This version compares it with the full text: Luft et al. introduce the correction factor (their eq. 26) and a scaled variant (eq. 28), and prove that two-robot blocks stay positive definite (Proposition 1, now credited at Theorem 8.1 and Corollary 5.3); they make no claim about boundedness or convergence of the covariance and give no divergence example. The two citing works are now also compared in full text. No theorem, proof, certificate, computation or numerical finding changed. Archive: LaTeX manuscript and PDF, bibliography with registry records, exact rational verifiers, interval certificates C1–C3, numerical scripts and their outputs (normal and python -O), figures, CI and SHA-256 manifest. Assurance: internal AI-assisted review only (not human peer review, independent reproduction or formal verification); certificates are computer-assisted, not formal proofs. Creator: Anonymous. Text CC0-1.0; code MIT.

items.summary: Repeated mobile GUI tests can reuse routes, locators, and recovery strategies from earlier executions. However, a route that worked in one workflow or app version may be irrelevant or misleading in another. We study how an LLM-based tester can retain useful experience while withholding entries contradicted by current observations. We present a maintenance contract for AdaptiTest in which reusable experience has an explicit applicability scope, trace provenance, and a lifecycle for confirmation, revalidation, and withdrawal. The contract reserves persistence for a Reflector role and treats recalled experience as advice. The archived implementation does not establish end-to-end enforcement of every specified mechanism. The design changes retrieved context, not model weights. The evaluation uses read-only Android workflows and archived internal comparisons. A six-task, three-repeat ready subset reports 18/18 completed runs with memory versus 3/18 without it, but a grounded single-agent control also solves the earlier hard-task slice. A separate cross-session probe is excluded from efficacy conclusions because of confounded route schedules and unvalidated state labels. We examine 13 selected real-update hazard records across nine subjects, distinguishing stale-locator observations from policy-based withholding and offline retrieval diagnostics. The latter do not measure live-device failures or actions saved. These events are UI changes, not confirmed regression bugs. The evidence supports a bounded design and case study; it does not establish general efficacy, superiority over independent GUI-agent systems, or unrestricted exploration.
items.title: Can LLM Agents Learn to Test? Maintaining Scoped Experience as Testing Evidence for Mobile GUI Testing

items.summary: Patient world models are increasingly proposed as simulators of clinical trials, and recent surveys rank their capabilities on a ladder from temporal prediction to counterfactual rollouts. Position on that ladder is currently assigned by reading papers rather than by measurement. We turn the counterfactual rung into a measured quantity. From 30,119 completed phase 2/3 trials with results posted to ClinicalTrials.gov we construct 9,996 audited within-trial contrasts from 7,207 trials, and we score a simulator on how much of its accuracy depends on knowing which intervention was tested. The instrument is an intervention-blind reference: the same model, trained on the same trials, with every intervention-identifying field withheld. Interventional skill is the error the full model removes relative to that reference. On a temporal split (878 test contrasts from 655 trials) a registry-trained gradient-boosting simulator removes a fifth of the error of a trivial baseline, but its interventional skill is -0.12 (95% CI -0.21 to -0.05): withholding the intervention makes it better, and no alternative featurisation, stratum, temporal cut or same-molecule retrieval yields an interval above zero. A frontier language model reading only the registered protocol has interventional skill 0.20 [0.08, 0.31]; smaller and open-weight models sit at the limit of detection. Perturbation tests show the large model uses the intervention as such: swapping the arms reverses the sign of its prediction in 86% of contrasts. The blind reference is itself not drug-blind (a language model recovers the withheld drug class 45% of the time from the blind prompt), so interventional skill is a conservative lower bound. A reliability layer shows that ranking by predicted error lowers it but that calibrated error control does not transfer under temporal shift. Benchmark, code, prompts and per-call model outputs are released.
items.title: Does Your Trial Simulator Know What the Drug Does? An Intervention-Blind Test of Interventional Validity on 7,207 Registered Trials

items.summary: Real-world geospatial decision support requires more than single-step retrieval or code generation. Disaster-response questions often involve multi-source workflows that combine spatial databases, map-derived features, satellite imagery, raster products, and reusable geospatial artifacts, where correctness depends on preserving spatial scope, temporal context, and intermediate execution state. While large language models and coding agents offer a promising interface for such workflows, they struggle with geospatial-specific failure modes, including handling large artifacts, selecting the wrong evidence source, losing spatial or temporal metadata, and applying invalid geometric operations. We introduce GeoFaham, a domain-specialized multi-agent system for geospatial disaster analytics. GeoFaham decomposes workflows into specialist agents for vector operations, map feature retrieval, imagery discovery, and raster analysis, coordinated by an Orchestrator with a dual-ledger control loop for dependency-aware planning, progress tracking, validation, and replanning. To support artifact-centric collaboration, GeoFaham uses a Response Store that persists full geospatial outputs and typed metadata outside the LLM context window while agents exchange compact identifiers and summaries. We also introduce GeoFaham-Bench, a 40-task benchmark grounded in 17 real-world disaster records, designed to evaluate multi-step geospatial reasoning, cross-source integration, raster-vector computation, artifact generation, and recovery under non-rigid ground truth. We evaluate GeoFaham on GeoFaham-Bench against strong general-purpose coding-agent baselines, including Codex, Claude Code, and OpenCode. GeoFaham achieves the best overall performance, scoring 0.940 versus the next-best 0.879, while using 7.5 times fewer tokens. Our code and benchmark are publicly available at https://github.com/microsoft/GeoFaham.
items.title: GeoFaham: Domain-Specialized Multi-Agent Geospatial Analytics for Disaster Response

items.summary: Overview: This deposit hosts the official replication package, synthetic benchmark dataset, and experimental audit artifacts for the scientific manuscript: "M-11: Auditing Synthetic Risk Labels and Physical Baselines in a Cyber-Physical Benchmark for Underground Mining" (submitted to Acta Montanistica Slovaca , 2026). M-11 is a simulation-only cyber-physical benchmark that integrates AI4I 2020 predictive maintenance attributes with synthetic kinematic positioning, physiological, and environmental indicators (10,000 records; 37 columns) to audit the statistical mechanics and potential circularity of synthetic risk labelling in confined underground mining operations. Key Empirical Findings Reported in the Manuscript: Label Circularity Audit: Variance decomposition demonstrates that 82.07% of the synthetic score variance is driven by spatial/kinematic components, 17.43% by injected noise, 0.48% by multimodal variables, and 0.02% by cross-covariance. Symmetric Holdout Evaluation (n = 2,000; seed 42): Calibrated Time-to-Collision (TTC) and Random Forest both achieve F2 = 0.9103; XGBoost achieves F2 = 0.9065. The paired bootstrap difference (ΔF2 = -0.0038, 95% CI: -0.0129 to 0.0047) and Holm-adjusted McNemar test (p = 0.6015) confirm no statistically significant gap under circular labels. Decoupled Hazard Stress Tests: Under 22% class prevalence and low signal-to-noise ratio, non-spatial decoupled labels (CO, fatigue, vibration) push F2 optimisation to near-universal HIGH alerts, approaching the trivial Always-HIGH baseline (F2 = 0.5851). A multimodal-only composite target recovers F2 = 0.6408 with 54.1% specificity. Feature Ablations: Removing three direct kinematic indicators reduces F2 by 9.60 percentage points; removing the entire 8-feature spatial block reduces F2 by 32.52 percentage points from the full 0.9065 baseline. Computational Scalability: Local backend P95 latency scales to 27.91 ms under 500 concurrent simulated agents (< 200 ms supervisory threshold). The WebGL/Three.js integrated-GPU prototype achieves 34.8 FPS under nominal load. Deterministic Safety & GenAI Audit: The independent deterministic safety layer satisfies 17 automated unit/integration tests and 100/100 scripted regulatory scenario checks. The Gemini language model acts strictly as an exploratory natural-language interface without numerical autonomy. Package Contents & Cryptographic Verification (SHA-256): public_mining_equipment_dataset.csv (3,859,401 bytes) — SHA-256: b71d0b6baed8b6e0bc7eee1a1a5b7440d06a04ddaea5d502907cf03d958705f0 requirements.txt (574 bytes) — Frozen Python 3.10.11 scientific environment specifications. results/feature_dictionary.csv (2,928 bytes) — Full data dictionary defining all 37 attributes, physical units, and provenance. results/label_circularity_audit.json (17,530 bytes) — Machine-readable variance decomposition and baseline comparison exports. results/genai_audit_bank.json (35,882 bytes) — 100 structured synthetic scenarios for LLM compliance auditing. results/genai_audit_review_sheet.csv (47,295 bytes) — Manual verification rubric with inter-annotator agreement (Cohen's κ = 0.85). Boundary of Scope: M-11 is a computational simulation benchmark and exploratory supervisory prototype. It does not establish mine-site functional safety, nor does it claim active-mine physical twin synchronisation or autonomous braking actuation.

items.summary: This record contains the code, a simulated benchmark dataset, and the result files for a study on detecting cyberattacks that are masked by AI data-center load transients in inverter-rich distribution grids. The manuscript itself is not included. Benchmark. The IEEE 33-bus distribution feeder is driven by 61 measured GPU power traces: 10 large-language-model training runs and 51 inference runs, recorded on A100, H100, H200 and L40S GPUs at 0.1 s. These traces form the load of an AI data center at bus 7, rated at 15–30% of feeder load. A photovoltaic inverter at bus 17 follows the IEEE 1547-2018 Category B volt-var curve. Nine channels are recorded at 10 Hz: three bus voltages, feeder-head P and Q, data-center P and Q, and inverter P and Q. The dataset holds 1,000 labeled scenarios of 120 s each. Of these, 598 contain one of seven attack types (bias, scaling, ramp, pulse, replay, coordinated mimic, and control-loop), and 220 of the attacks are hidden inside data-center load transients. Every sample is labeled for attack and for load transient. Code. The Python code covers: a linearized DistFlow model and an exact AC backward/forward-sweep power flow; data-center load generation from the GPU traces; attack injection and 10 Hz scenario simulation; physics-residual features learned from historical measurements, without feeder impedances; the RIME optimizer and a CNN-LSTM-attention detector (PR-Net); gradient-boosting, random-forest, MLP and logistic-regression baselines; window-level and event-level evaluation with scenario-bootstrap confidence intervals. Results. The result files contain the numbers behind all tables and figures: comparisons of detectors trained with and without load-transient awareness and physics residuals; ablations, computational cost, and an equal-budget comparison of RIME, random search and an untuned default; robustness tests under seven conditions, including exact AC power flow, unseen workload shapes, and changes in noise, photovoltaic share, data-center size and inverter location; a replay-attack consistency check; trained Stage-1 network weights. Third-party data. The GPU power traces come from the public LLM Power Trace Explorer repository (commit 9c25218). Because that repository has no license file, the raw traces are not redistributed here; scripts/prepare_gpu_traces.py rebuilds them from the public source. The included benchmark contains only simulated feeder signals driven by normalized, scaled versions of those load shapes.

items.summary: Flapping-wing simulation must reconcile high-frequency wingbeat aerodynamics with the slower dynamics relevant to flight control and reinforcement learning. We present FlapSim, a modular open-source MuJoCo simulation platform that combines robot descriptions, wing geometry, and composable aerodynamic models in a deterministic simulation pipeline. Across $48$ held-out scenarios spanning frequency, gimbal, wind, frequency-step, gust, and cross-robot flat-plate regimes, we compare five reduced-order configurations operating at $1\,\text{ms}$ with a $50\,μ\text{s}$ quasi-steady blade-element reference. The built-in hover cycle-averaged baseline achieves a $67.51\times$ CPU speedup but only $0.6593$ mean wrench fidelity. Combining multirate $21$-substep clock synchronization, three-dimensional linear/quadratic inflow and gust coupling, analytical blade-element geometry scaling, and phase-locked $1f\text{--}6f$ harmonics raises mean fidelity to $0.9646$ at a $65.19\times$ speedup in a five-block model. A streamlined four-block model without explicit step-transient lag states achieves $0.9662$ fidelity at a $67.98\times$ speedup. Controlled ablations show that stroke harmonics are particularly important during frequency transitions, improving held-out frequency-step fidelity by $+0.3176$. Transfer-function analysis explains this effect: fixed-window cycle averaging retains harmonic contributions when the wingbeat frequency changes, so within-cycle reconstruction also improves the filtered wrench. Once phase alignment and harmonic synthesis are included, explicit transient lag states provide no additional benefit in this benchmark. These results characterize the accuracy--computation tradeoff of the aerodynamic hierarchy and identify timing, inflow, geometry, and harmonic representation as central considerations for reduced-order flapping-wing simulation.
items.title: FlapSim: A Composable MuJoCo Simulation Platform and Reduced-Order Aerodynamic Model Hierarchy for Flapping-Wing Robotics

items.summary: Frontier LLM agents can turn known vulnerabilities into working exploits, but are costly and often access-restricted due to their potential for malicious use. Open-weight models offer a more accessible alternative, but struggle to maintain progress across long exploitation chains. They also often fail to apply relevant security knowledge at the appropriate stage and in the right context to identify and evaluate promising attack directions. To address these limitations, we propose DoGNAVY-Exploit, a multi-agent harness built around two complementary designs: stage-aware decomposition with progressive expert knowledge disclosure, and hierarchical orchestration with parallel exploration. Specifically, DoGNAVY-Exploit uses configurable milestones to recast long-horizon exploitation as short, verifiable capability transitions and provides only the knowledge relevant to each stage. Within each milestone, a hierarchical architecture separates strategic planning from parallel execution: a planner proposes diverse attack routes, executors test them concurrently, and a controller accepts progress only when supported by runtime evidence. A shared structured memory consolidates verified facts, artifacts, replay steps, and failed routes across branches, allowing agents to build on collective progress and carry validated knowledge into subsequent milestones. In controlled benchmark environments, DoGNAVY-Exploit with GLM-5.2 achieves 97.5% Pass@1 on Cybench, and 97.5% zero-day and 100% one-day Pass@1 on CVE-Bench. On ExploitGym, it solves 79 tasks with GLM-5.2 and 157 with GLM-5.3, while the corresponding public Claude Code baselines solve 39 and 130 tasks, respectively. Ablation results further demonstrate that the stage-aware orchestration, expert knowledge, parallel exploration, and memory designs can substantially improve the exploitation capabilities of open-weight agents.
items.title: DoGNAVY-Exploit: Harnessing Parallel Open-Weight Agents for Stage-Aware Vulnerability Exploitation

items.summary: This package reproduces all tables and figures of the article “Completing Ecosystem Knowledge Graphs: Few-Shot Learning with Calibrated Rules and the Governance of Innovative Start-ups”. The article builds LUCE-KG, an ontology-rich knowledge graph of 15,493 Italian innovative start-ups and SMEs and 25,982 persons. It proposes CRML, a few-shot learner whose predictions are explained by rules with empirical-Bayes calibrated confidences, and tests it on four graphs (FB15k-237, CoDEx-M, NELL-One and LUCE-KG). It then analyses 11,764 firm-years with panel estimators, clustering and explained machine-learning models. Contents code/ : the full pipeline, from graph construction through few-shot completion, baselines (MetaR, TransE, AnyBURL, LLM re-ranking), econometrics, clustering and machine learning, to the build of the manuscript; config/ : few-shot splits, fold assignments, selected hyperparameters and the LUCE-KG ontology; results/ : aggregated results from which every table is built; data_open/ : open-data extracts of the Italian register of innovative start-ups and SMEs (July 2026); README.md with the order of execution, and requirements.txt with software versions. Data not included. Officer and financial records from AIDA (Bureau van Dijk) are licensed and contain personal data, so they are not redistributed. Licensed users can rebuild every input with the scripts provided. The public benchmarks are available from their original sources. Environment. CPU only (2 cores, 8 GB RAM), Python 3.13; the full pipeline takes about 40 CPU-hours. Funding. Project “LUtech Campus Ecosystem—LUCE” (Project Code 22ROJB5), Puglia Region, Program Agreement (Contratto di Programma).

items.summary: Biological discovery requires using molecular knowledge and new measurements to infer responses beyond the conditions already observed. We introduce CellCanon, the first agentic cellular world model to unify single-cell expression prediction, evidence-grounded explanation, and observation-driven updating. Its predictive core reuses condition-level biological evidence across gene-specific numerical readouts to guide single-cell expression generation. A shared world state links predictions, acquired measurements, and source-linked claims, supporting explanation and revision. On 339 held-out SciPlex3 conditions across three cell lines, CellCanon improves differential-expression AUPRC and Macro-F1 over the best baseline for each metric by 63.3% and 17.3%, respectively, and direction Macro-F1 by 7.2%. Relative to gene-wise reasoning on matched drug-cell cohorts, measured language-model token use falls by 99.77% for Predict and 98.41% for Explain. On the source-grounded benchmark, Explain correctly answers all answerable questions with supporting proofs and identifies all insufficient-evidence cases. In simulated experimental feedback, Update uses one measured source context per drug to exceed the best fine-tuned baselines in differential-expression AUPRC and Macro-F1 without changing model weights. Together, these capabilities support a cumulative account of cellular responses, with predictions and biological judgments that can be revised as evidence accumulates.
items.title: CellCanon: An Agentic Cellular World Model for Prediction, Explanation, and Observation-Driven Updating

items.summary: This article connects demographic renewal with multinational recruitment control and the operating life of committed capital. Its host-choice argument engages resource bundling and global staffing, with explicit conditions for shared recruitment, competition and border disruption. Version 3.65.0 adds a Bayesian decision analysis to the Nitra–Puebla staffing appraisal. Under the existing flat-margin, equal-offer-odds benchmark, choosing Nitra after losing the whole UK route carries an expected loss from choosing the wrong host of EUR0.14–1.00 million. Losing only intakes after year fourteen reduces that expected loss to about EUR2,000–15,000. Nitra retains the higher expected value in these reference comparisons. Appendix K11 derives the decision rule, reports alternative priors and provides two independent integrations of 312 specifications. These are conditional public-information appraisals before capital commitment, not realised JLR losses or evidence about its internal contracts. Existing Bayesian panel estimates, demographic inputs, propositions and eight figures are retained. The article distinguishes the measured population-access specification from the recruitment-control mechanism and explains common tenure through the timing of workforce replacement. No observations or regressions are added. Start with Main_Manuscript_ANONYMOUS.pdf, Online_Appendix_ANONYMOUS.pdf and README.txt. Compilable sources, public inputs, code, figure files and aggregate outputs are supplied. The current replication overlay and nine frozen base archives restore the complete permitted replication. Licensed WRDS rows require subscriber access; queries and reconstruction instructions are supplied. Editor-only cover and title pages are excluded.

items.summary: Long-horizon multi-agent systems suffer from three tightly coupled failures: task drift, role drift, and state staleness. We test the hypothesis that these share a common representational cause: agent hidden states move away from the directions encoding the active task, assigned role, and current shared state. A pilot study over 14,832 annotated turns supports this: drifted turns collapse near-uniformly across all three anchor subspaces (pairwise r = 0.72-0.78). Existing methods address these failures separately, operating at the surface-text level or treating control directions independently. We introduce ATLAS (Algebraic Task-role Locking with Adaptive Spectral Memory), a training-free intervention acting on hidden states before a token is generated. ATLAS builds a positive-semidefinite anchor kernel over task, role, and state subspaces and steers hidden states toward their shared high-coherence eigendirections; a low-rank Gram decomposition keeps this tractable. Across long-horizon memory, state maintenance, tool use, least-privilege coordination, and embodied stress tests, ATLAS outperforms prompting, retrieval, memory, and activation-steering baselines. Against A-MEM it improves memory macro-average accuracy by up to 5.7 points and reduces write/read failures by up to 31.7%/24.8%; against MemoryArena-Agent it gains up to 4.8 points. It gains 10.7-12.1 points under perturbation, reaches 93.5% role consistency, and transfers to a 72B backbone (macro-average 61.0 vs. 56.2). Ablating the joint task-role-state span costs 7.2 points against 0.8 for a matched-rank random span, indicating these directions are functionally implicated, not incidental; supplying them by prompt or retrieval recovers 4.3 points less. ATLAS is therefore a representation-level controller for open-weight multi-agent systems, complementary to output-level protocols for black-box agents.
items.title: Drift No More: Spectral Locking for Long-Horizon Open-Weight Multi-Agent AI

items.summary: Patient world models are increasingly proposed as simulators of clinical trials, and recent surveys rank their capabilities on a ladder from temporal prediction to counterfactual rollouts. Position on that ladder is currently assigned by reading papers rather than by measurement. We turn the counterfactual rung into a measured quantity. From 30,119 completed phase 2/3 trials with results posted to ClinicalTrials.gov we construct 9,996 audited within-trial contrasts from 7,207 trials, and we score a simulator on how much of its accuracy depends on knowing which intervention was tested. The instrument is an intervention-blind reference: the same model, trained on the same trials, with every intervention-identifying field withheld. Interventional skill is the error the full model removes relative to that reference. On a temporal split (878 test contrasts from 655 trials) a registry-trained gradient-boosting simulator removes a fifth of the error of a trivial baseline, but its interventional skill is -0.12 (95% CI -0.21 to -0.05): withholding the intervention makes it better, and no alternative featurisation, stratum, temporal cut or same-molecule retrieval yields an interval above zero. A frontier language model reading only the registered protocol has interventional skill 0.20 [0.08, 0.31]; smaller and open-weight models sit at the limit of detection. Perturbation tests show the large model uses the intervention as such: swapping the arms reverses the sign of its prediction in 86% of contrasts. The blind reference is itself not drug-blind (a language model recovers the withheld drug class 45% of the time from the blind prompt), so interventional skill is a conservative lower bound. A reliability layer shows that ranking by predicted error lowers it but that calibrated error control does not transfer under temporal shift. Benchmark, code, prompts and per-call model outputs are released.
items.title: Does Your Trial Simulator Know What the Drug Does? An Intervention-Blind Test of Interventional Validity on 7,207 Registered Trials
